title: Durga Comes Home
hookLine: a mother at a window, watching the road for a daughter who also rides a lion
carry: the almighty goddess, loved as a daughter
tomorrow: a dark goddess on a kitchen wall, and a grandmother who says ma

cards: A woman stands at a window, watching the road. A year ago her daughter married and moved far up into the mountains, to a husband who smears himself with ash and has no house to speak of.

Now autumn is here, and the daughter is coming home for a few days, bringing the children. The mother has been cooking since morning. She is Menaka, queen of the mountains, in songs people sing in Bengal.
And the daughter she's waiting for rides a lion. A new stretch begins: five goddesses, met not as titles but as characters.

teach.b: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati. Over the next days, this path meets them one at a time, the way you'd get to know people.

Some Hindus hear all five as faces of one great Goddess, the way the Devi Mahatmya's goddesses walked back into one. Others hold one of them close as their own. This path tells the stories and leaves that to each family.
Start with Durga. In the Devi Mahatmya she's the one the gods can't do without. When the buffalo demon has beaten them, their combined radiance becomes her, and each god hands her a weapon.

teach.h: DURGA: SHAKTI, THE POWER OF THE GODS.
teach.b: Hindus call that power Shakti, and in this tradition Shakti is the Goddess herself. She laughs in battle. She doesn't need rescuing; she is the rescue.
But in Bengal, at Durga Puja, she is also somebody's daughter. Tradition there says she is Uma, born to the mountain king and queen, married to Shiva, and once a year she comes home to her parents.
Old songs called agamani are sung in her mother's voice: the waiting, the worry, the joy at the gate.
When the festival ends, there are songs of farewell as the image is carried to the water, and people say goodbye the way a family says goodbye to a married daughter going back to her husband's house.
So one goddess holds two pictures: the warrior with a weapon in every hand, and the girl whose mother has been at the window all morning. That's a real Hindu teaching, not just a sweet custom.
In bhakti, devotion, you may love God through a human bond: as a child, a friend, a beloved, even your own daughter. Bengal loves the power behind the universe as its girl, and cries when she leaves.

how: In Bengal, Durga Puja is kept as both a celebration of the goddess's victory and a homecoming: families welcome Durga as a married daughter visiting her parents, and on the last day the clay images are carried to a river or pond for immersion.

games.q: you're Menaka, queen of the mountains. your daughter married an ash-covered ascetic and moved away. autumn comes. what do the songs show you doing?
o: forgetting her, since she's married now
waiting at the window, watching the road

games.why: the agamani songs are sung in the mother's voice: the waiting, the worry, and the joy when the daughter comes home with her children.

practice: At Durga Puja, people offer anjali: flowers held in folded hands, offered toward the Goddess as the priest chants.
Fold your hands that way now, and for a few breaths picture her both ways: mighty enough to save the gods, close enough to come home for dinner.
If you pray, offer the flowers in your heart to Ma Durga; if you don't, let the open hands be enough.

wordCard.voice: Durga. The goddess the gods couldn't do without, and in Bengal's songs, a daughter coming home. The first of five characters. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Durga. In the Devi Mahatmya's eleventh chapter, the goddess says she will take this name after slaying a demon called Durgama.

carryVoice: Your line: the almighty goddess, loved as a daughter. Tomorrow, Kali, on a kitchen wall. Until tomorrow.
